# Figures, Tables, and the Index {#sec-chapter2}

The floats and the back-of-book index, which is the one feature of this
template that needs a little care.

## Figures

An image with an identifier becomes a numbered, referenceable figure:

``` markdown
![A placeholder figure.](example-figure.pdf){#fig-example width=70%}
```

![A placeholder figure.](example-figure.pdf){#fig-example width=70%}

@fig-example refers to it. `width=` accepts a percentage of the text
width, and `fig-align="center"` centres a figure narrower than the text
block. PDF and PNG both work; vector PDF is better for line art.

## Tables

A pipe table with a caption line becomes a numbered table. The caption
carries the identifier:

| Variable        |  Mean |    SD |
|:----------------|------:|------:|
| Outcome $y$     |  0.50 |  0.10 |
| Regressor $x$   |  0.00 |  1.00 |
| Control $z$     |  0.00 |  1.00 |

: Descriptive statistics. {#tbl-summary}

@tbl-summary refers to it. Colons in the header separator set the column
alignment: `:---` left, `---:` right, `:---:` centred. The template loads
**booktabs**, so rules come out at the right weights without any manual
`\hline`.

Long tables split across pages automatically. If a table is wider than the
text block, set the column widths explicitly with `tbl-colwidths`:

``` markdown
: A wide table. {#tbl-wide tbl-colwidths="[60,20,20]"}
```

## The index

The template loads **makeidx** and prints the index at the end of the
book. Nothing appears there until you mark terms. `\index{}` is raw LaTeX
and goes immediately after the word it indexes, with no space:

``` markdown
The assumption of stationarity\index{stationarity} is maintained
throughout, as is linearity\index{models!linear}.
```

The assumption of stationarity\index{stationarity} is maintained
throughout, as is linearity\index{models!linear}.

An exclamation mark makes a subentry, so `models!linear` files "linear"
under a "models" heading. The index is built during the render --- there
is no separate `makeindex` step to run --- and it lists the page each
marked term fell on, which is why the entries above point at this page.

`\index{}` is dropped silently in the HTML build rather than printed as
stray text, so marking terms is safe even if HTML is your main output.

## Code

Fenced blocks are set in Source Code Pro and are not executed unless you
use an executable chunk:

``` r
fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)
summary(fit)
```

For output that runs at render time, use a `{r}` chunk. That needs
**knitr**, and the file extension stays `.qmd`.

## Content for one format only

Some material belongs in one output and not the other --- a full-page
LaTeX table in print, an interactive widget on the web:

``` markdown
::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
This paragraph appears only in the PDF.
:::
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
This paragraph appears only in the PDF, which is where you are reading it.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
This paragraph appears only in the HTML build.
:::

The dedication page in `index.qmd` uses the same mechanism, with a
centred LaTeX block for print and a styled div for the web.
